The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Aharon Berechiah of Modena
Introduction and Period of Activity: The Historical and Spiritual Background in Northern Italy
The late sixteenth century and the first half of the seventeenth century were marked by a profound transformation in the spiritual and communal life of the Jewish communities of northern Italy [cite: 1, 2]. Torah centers in cities such as Mantua, Venice, Modena and Reggio Emilia experienced an encounter between the splendid local heritage of Italian Jewry and the new mystical currents that had burst forth from the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 2, 3]. In this period the phenomenon of voluntary pietistic confraternities and associations intensified: gatherings of Torah scholars and early risers who laid down regulations for prayer in the morning watch, for rectifications of the soul and for organized charitable kindness [cite: 1, 2, 4].
Within this vibrant religious and social climate worked Rabbi Aharon Berechiah ben Moshe of Modena, one of the outstanding Italian sages of his generation [cite: 1, 3]. His work embodies a central connecting link between the Kabbalah of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (the Ramak) and the penetration of the Kabbalah of Rabbi Isaac Luria (the Ari) into the European sphere [cite: 1, 3, 5]. Rabbi Aharon Berechiah united in his person halakhic authority, communal leadership, liturgical poetry and liturgy, alongside profound mystical contemplation [cite: 1, 3, 6]. His principal work, the book Maavar Yabbok (The Crossing of the Jabbok), redefined the attitude of Jewish society toward states of illness, dying, death and mourning, and became the undisputed foundational book of the burial societies (chevrot kadisha) throughout the Jewish diaspora [cite: 4, 6, 7, 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life, Family Background and Ordination
Rabbi Aharon Berechiah son of Rabbi Moshe son of Rabbi Nehemiah was born in the city of Modena in northern Italy [cite: 1, 3, 8]. In the scholarly literature and in rabbinic historiography there are different versions regarding the year of his birth: some sources place it as early as the year 5309 (1549), and others as late as around the year 5348 (1585) [cite: 1, 3]. Rabbi Aharon Berechiah grew up in a distinguished and wealthy home; his mother, Mistress Imperia, came from an important family descended from the exiles of France, and his father, Rabbi Moshe, was one of the city's magnates and one of the community's powerful leaders [cite: 3]. In his childhood he was educated in the home of his maternal grandmother, Mistress Fiorita, widow of the sage Rabbi Shlomo Yaakov Raphael [cite: 3].
The family atmosphere of study and creativity shaped his character from a young age. Rabbi Aharon Berechiah was the cousin (on his mother's side) of the renowned rabbi and scholar Rabbi Yehuda Aryeh of Modena (Leon Modena) [cite: 1, 8, 9], and the brother-in-law of the Kabbalist and liturgical poet Rabbi Yosef Yedidyah Karmi, author of Kenaf Renanim [cite: 1, 8, 10]. In the year 5370 (1610) he was ordained to issue rulings with the ordination of the sages of Safed by Rabbi Yom Tov Tzahalon (the Maharitatz), who had come to Modena as an emissary of the rabbis from the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 3]. This ordination testified to broad recognition of his Torah authority.
After his ordination he established a yeshiva and a Talmud Torah in his home, in which he disseminated Torah to many [cite: 3]. Later he founded a synagogue and a beit midrash in his father's house, and even received an official tax exemption from the Duke of Modena for his institutions [cite: 3]. Rabbi Aharon Berechiah had sons and a daughter, and the best known of them was his son Rabbi Hillel, who was one of the sages of Modena [cite: 3]. As part of the phenomenon of mystical revelations characteristic of the Kabbalists of the period, Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai (the Chida) noted that according to tradition Rabbi Aharon Berechiah merited the revelation of a heavenly maggid who taught him secrets of the Torah [cite: 3, 5, 8]. Rabbi Aharon Berechiah died in Modena on 26 Tammuz 5399 (28 July 1639) [cite: 1, 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Teachers and His Spiritual and Kabbalistic Sources
The Torah and Kabbalistic teaching of Rabbi Aharon Berechiah rests on the legacy of the great figures of the generation in Italy, who bequeathed to him the foundations of the revealed Torah, of asceticism and of the hidden wisdom:
Rabbi Hillel the Pious of Modena: one of his principal teachers in his youth, from whom he acquired the foundations of the revealed Torah, asceticism and practical piety [cite: 1, 3, 5]. Rabbi Hillel, who was known by the title "the pious and holy," guided his disciple in the paths of asceticism and devekut (cleaving to God) [cite: 5].
Rabbi Menachem Azariah of Fano (the Rama of Fano): the greatest of the Italian Kabbalists, a head of a yeshiva and a renowned halakhic decisor [cite: 1, 2, 3, 5]. The Rama of Fano was Rabbi Aharon Berechiah's principal teacher in the wisdom of Kabbalah [cite: 1, 2, 3]. (In certain popular sources his figure was at times confused with that of the Kabbalist Rabbi Moshe Zacuto, the Ramaz, who was active in Italy in the following generation.) From the Rama of Fano Rabbi Aharon Berechiah received the liturgical and halakhic conception that combines the laws of the revealed Torah with the kavvanot (mystical intentions) of the hidden [cite: 2].
Rabbi Israel Sarug: a disciple of the Ari, who came to Italy and was among the first disseminators of the Kabbalah of the Ari in Europe [cite: 1, 3, 8]. Rabbi Aharon Berechiah studied with him and became a central transmitter of the Sarugian-Lurianic version [cite: 1, 3, 8].
These sources produced in Rabbi Aharon Berechiah a complex system that fused Cordoverian depth with the Lurianic structures of the partzufim and the kavvanot [cite: 1, 3, 5].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Literary Work and the Controversies over Prayer Text and Liturgy
The literary work of Rabbi Aharon Berechiah includes compositions printed during his lifetime and after his death, alongside many manuscripts that were brought to light by later sages [cite: 1, 3, 5, 8].
Title of the work | Year of printing / status | Description and main content
Ashmoret ha-Boker | Mantua 1624 (5384) | An order of prayers, selichot and supplications especially for the confraternity of "Me'irei ha-Shachar," those who rise early [cite: 1, 4, 5, 9].
Maavar Yabbok | Mantua 1626 (5386) | A comprehensive work addressing customs, prayers, laws and Kabbalistic secrets concerning illness, death and mourning [cite: 6, 7, 11].
Bigdei Kodesh | Pisa 1785 (5545) | Guidance and reflections on the order of study, the service of God and the kavvanot of prayer [cite: 3, 8, 9].
Me'il Tzedakah | Pisa 1785 (5545) | Sermons and guidance on the rectification of character traits, the virtue of charity and spiritual service [cite: 3, 8, 9].
Shemen Mishchat Kodesh | Manuscript | A Kabbalistic work on the principles of the wisdom of truth according to the Kabbalah of the Ramak and the Ari [cite: 5].
Shemen Zayit Zach | Manuscript | Discourses and rules in the wisdom of Kabbalah according to the teaching of the Ari [cite: 1, 5, 12].
Shatil Pore'ach | Manuscript | Kavvanot for prayers, the washing of the hands, dietary prohibitions and the holiness of the Sabbath [cite: 1, 5, 8].
Imrei Shefer | Manuscript | Novellae and profound explanations of Kabbalistic sayings [cite: 1, 5, 8].
Magen Aharon | Manuscript | An abridgment and comprehensive summary of the writings of the Ari [cite: 1, 5, 8].
Commentary on the Tikkunei ha-Zohar | Manuscript | A detailed Kabbalistic commentary on the book Tikkunei ha-Zohar [cite: 1, 5, 8].
In 1624 Rabbi Aharon Berechiah printed his work Ashmoret ha-Boker (also called Me'irei ha-Shachar), which was intended for the pietistic confraternity in Modena that was accustomed to rise before dawn [cite: 1, 4, 5, 9]. Three years later, in 1627, his brother-in-law, Rabbi Yosef Yedidyah Karmi, published the prayer book Kenaf Renanim [cite: 1, 10, 13].
A sharp controversy arose between the two, which was brought before the rabbinic court in Modena for a decision [cite: 1]. The dispute revolved around changes in the text of the prayers, the introduction of new confessions, and the incorporation of Kabbalistic kavvanot drawn from the Kabbalah of the Ari, as against the Italian prayer tradition and the rulings of the school of the Rama of Fano [cite: 1, 2, 10]. This controversy reflected the growing tension in Italy between preserving the custom of the communities and changing the liturgy under the influence of Lurianic Kabbalah [cite: 1, 2].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Book Maavar Yabbok: Structure, Contents and the Theology of the Crossing
The book Maavar Yabbok was first printed in Mantua in 1626 and became a canonical foundational work [cite: 6, 7]. The title of the book is derived from the crossing of the Jabbok River by Jacob Our Father in Genesis chapter 32 [cite: 6, 11, 14]. In his introduction the author develops a profound Kabbalistic allegory: the crossing of the river is expressed as the soul's passage across the boundary between this material world and the spiritual World to Come [cite: 11]. The struggle with the angel "until the break of dawn" is likened to the struggle of the soul with the forces of judgment and with the Angel of Death at the moment the soul departs, while the rising of the dawn symbolizes rectification, spiritual sunrise and the resurrection of the dead [cite: 6]. Likewise, the numerical value (gematria) of the book's name equals the number of its chapters, 112, and he interprets it as an acronym: Yichud (unification), Berakhah (blessing), Kedushah (holiness) [cite: 6, 7, 11].
The book is organized systematically and divided into five main parts, which the author calls "ma'amarot" (essays) [cite: 6, 11]:
1.  First essay, "Siftei Tzedek": devoted to the commandment of visiting the sick, the duty of supplication for the healing of the sick person, and the clarification of the concept of "outcry" that bursts forth from the heart and is equated to ten prayers for the sweetening of judgments [cite: 6, 11]. This part presents guidance for the sick person to accept the divine judgment as just, to repent, to confess, and to direct his intention to give his life for the sanctification of God's name [cite: 6].
2.  Second essay, "Sefat Emet": deals with conduct in the moments of dying and the departure of the soul, the preservation of the holiness of the surroundings, and the recitation of the verses of unification at the moment the soul passes away [cite: 6, 11].
3.  Third essay, "Siftei Renanot": details the order of washing the dead (tahara), dressing in the shrouds, the funeral and the burial, giving them the Kabbalistic meaning of driving away evil spirits and protecting the deceased [cite: 6, 11, 15].
4.  Fourth essay: a composite essay divided into three parts [cite: 6, 11]:Atar Anan ha-Ketoret: prayers and supplications for the sick person and the deceased [cite: 6, 11].Korban Ta'anit: orders of fasts and rectifications of the soul for those accompanying the deceased and for family members [cite: 6, 11].Minchat Aharon: Kabbalistic kavvanot and essays explaining the rites of mourning and purification [cite: 6, 11].

Korban Ta'anit: orders of fasts and rectifications of the soul for those accompanying the deceased and for family members [cite: 6, 11].

1.  Fifth essay, "Imrei No'am": theological reflections on providence, suffering, divine mercy, the secret of reincarnation (gilgul), chibbut ha-kever (the beating of the grave) and life after death [cite: 6, 11, 15].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Kabbalistic, Philosophical and Ethical Teaching
The teaching of Rabbi Aharon Berechiah is characterized by conferring a mystical status on halakhic and communal acts [cite: 6, 11]. For him the processes of illness and death are not perceived as merely physiological events, but as an arena of cosmic struggle between the forces of holiness and the forces of judgment [cite: 6]. Every act of the burial society, the recitation of verses of Psalms (such as "He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High") and the orders of purification act as channels for sweetening the judgments and raising the sparks [cite: 15, 16].
His thought displays a synthesis between the Kabbalah of the Ramak and the Kabbalah of the Ari [cite: 1, 3, 5]. He makes use of the Lurianic system of sefirot and partzufim as it was rendered by Rabbi Israel Sarug, but combines with it concepts that pass through the rational-mystical filter of the Rama of Fano [cite: 1, 2, 5]. Relying on the author of Akedat Yitzchak (Rabbi Yitzchak Arama), Rabbi Aharon Berechiah establishes that human reason must subordinate itself before divine revelation and the secret, yet at the same time he offers an orderly and reasoned homiletic structure [cite: 5, 6].
Alongside Kabbalistic contemplation, Rabbi Aharon Berechiah set forth a trenchant social-ethical conception [cite: 3]. In his sermons he emphasizes that commerce conducted in good faith and honesty constitutes a drawing down of abundance from the world of holiness (the secret of the sefirah of Malkhut), whereas money that comes through fraud and falsehood draws from the channels of the sitra achra and consumes one's possessions [cite: 3]. He likens the commandment of charity to a burning candle, from which the lighting of many torches does not diminish its light, and thereby he teaches that one who gives his money for commandments does not reduce his possessions [cite: 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Disciples, His Halakhic Influence and His Legacy for the Generations
Rabbi Aharon Berechiah raised prominent disciples who continued his Torah and Kabbalistic path in Italy and beyond:
Rabbi Hillel of Modena: his son and the continuer of his path in Torah and in the hidden wisdom [cite: 3].
Rabbi Shabbetai Be'er: author of the book Be'er Esek, one of the great sages of Italy [cite: 17]. Rabbi Shabbetai studied Kabbalah with Rabbi Aharon Berechiah and with the Rama of Fano (and married the daughter of the Rama of Fano) [cite: 17]. Later he immigrated to the Land of Israel and served as a leader in the Jerusalem community [cite: 17].
The influence of the book Maavar Yabbok on the world of halakha and custom is immense. Although it was not written in the format of a classic book of rulings, the work became the central source of authority for halakhic decisors of all communities [cite: 6, 8]. The sages of Ashkenaz and Sepharad adopted its rulings and customs; thus, for example, the Ben Ish Chai (Rabbi Yosef Chaim of Baghdad) adopted many customs from Maavar Yabbok, noting that although they do not appear explicitly in the writings of the Ari, "a great man said the thing, namely the author of Maavar Yabbok, who was a great Kabbalist; therefore it is fitting to act thus" [cite: 18].
The book was printed in many editions (such as in Amsterdam 1732 and in Vilna 1860) and became the constant handbook of the burial societies [cite: 4, 6, 8]. Abridgments of the book were translated into Yiddish (such as the adaptation by Mistress Ellush bat Mordechai) and were made accessible to the general public and to women [cite: 6, 14].
The echo of Maavar Yabbok went beyond the bounds of the beit midrash and left a marked imprint on modern Hebrew and Yiddish literature [cite: 14]. Writers such as I. L. Peretz (in the story "Ha-Ilemet," "The Mute Woman") and Sholem Aleichem (in the story "Maavar Bug") incorporated the book as an element lending authenticity and emotional depth to scenes of dying and of longing for rectification [cite: 14]. The poet Shimon Halkin titled a collection of his poetry Maavar Yabbok, and Natan Alterman used this image in "Shir Asarah Achim" ("Song of Ten Brothers") to describe the crossing between life and death [cite: 14]. As an expression of historical recognition of his legacy, the Tel Aviv-Jaffa municipality named a street "Maavar Yabbok" in the Nachalat Yitzhak neighborhood, near the cemetery [cite: 6].
